facts.statement: The genus Rolfodon was described by Cappetta, Morrison, and Adnet in 2019.
Rolfodon is an extinct genus of shark belonging to the family Chlamydoselachidae.
facts.quote: Rolfodon is an extinct genus of shark in the family Chlamydoselachidae.

facts.statement: Rolfodon is closely related to modern frilled sharks but can be distinguished from them by differences in tooth shape.
facts.quote: It is closely related to the extant frilled sharks in the genus Chlamydoselachus, which it can be differentiated from by tooth morphology.

facts.statement: The earliest known fossil teeth of Rolfodon date to the Late Cretaceous Turonian/Santonian boundary in Japan.
facts.quote: The earliest fossil teeth of Rolfodon are known from the Late Cretaceous (Turonian/Santonian boundary) of Japan

facts.statement: Fossil remains of Rolfodon have been found worldwide, including Japan, Canada, Austria, New Zealand, Angola, Ecuador, and Antarctica.
facts.quote: Remains are known from worldwide, including Japan, Canada, Austria, New Zealand, Angola, Ecuador, and Antarctica.

facts.statement: The species R. goliath, found in the Late Campanian of Angola, could grow to very large sizes.
facts.quote: R. goliath, from the Late Campanian of Angola's southern Benguela Basin, could grow to very large sizes.

facts.statement: The holotype tooth of R. goliath is about 20mm high and features straightened, upright cusps with smooth, unornamented enameloid.
facts.quote: This tooth is about 20mm high, and is characterised by straightened, upright cusps with smooth enameloid which lack ornamentation.

facts.statement: The species R. tatere survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction, with fossils extending its known existence by over 10 million years from the Late Cretaceous of Antarctica to the Early Paleocene of New Zealand.
facts.quote: One individual species is also known to have survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event: R. tatere, which was first described from the Early Paleocene of New Zealand and was later also identified from the Late Cretaceous of Antarctica, extending the record of its existence by over 10 million years.

facts.statement: Most species of Rolfodon were previously classified within the genus Chlamydoselachus.
facts.quote: The majority of these species were previously classified in Chlamydoselachus.

facts.statement: The species Chlamydoselachus baumgartneri was moved to the separate genus Proteothrinax in 2012.
facts.quote: One species, Chlamydoselachus baumgartneri, was moved to its own genus Proteothrinax in 2012.

facts.statement: Research by Cappetta et al. in 2019 determined that the species formerly known as C. fiedleri actually belongs to the genus Rolfodon.
facts.quote: P. baumgartneri was later found to be conspecific with the previously described C. fiedleri, but fiedleri was found to belong to Rolfodon by Cappeta et al (2019).

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Rolfodon is Rolfodon ludvigseni.
Rolfodon lived from the Campanian to the Tortonian, spanning from 83.6 to 7.246 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Tortonian (83.6 to 7.246 million years ago)
